title: Developers still build parking where buyers want it; minimums only bind where demand is below the mandate
oneLiner: A minimum changes nothing where people want cars, and forces waste where they do not.
body: In car-dependent suburbs, apartments without parking do not sell, so developers build it whether or not it is required. The minimum only has an effect where buyers would accept less parking than the rule demands, which is exactly where it is most costly and least useful.
contextBackground: This is the market-logic version of the case for removal and the reason the Auckland result is not surprising to its supporters: provision fell where demand was lower and held where it was not.
contextDisagreement: Opponents argue developers under-provide because the spillover cost falls on neighbours, not on the building, so the market signal is incomplete. Whether that externality is large is the dispute.

otherClaim.title: Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing

claimItself.title: Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether planning schemes should stop requiring a set number of car spaces per new dwelling and let builders decide.
claimItself.body: Most Australian planning schemes require new apartments and townhouses to include a minimum number of off-street car spaces, typically one or more per dwelling. The proposal removes the minimum. Developers could still build parking; they would no longer be required to.

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Parking minimums add roughly $70,000 to the cost of a two-bedroom apartment in Sydney, $62,000 in Melbourne and up to $137,000 in Perth

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Auckland removed minimum parking requirements citywide in 2016, and new developments near frequent transit have since provided markedly less parking

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade

usedIn.relationSentence: This claim supports “Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing”

strengthDefinitions.decisive: The parent claim largely stands or falls on this one.
strengthDefinitions.relevant: It adds real weight, but the parent claim survives without it.
strengthDefinitions.tangential: True perhaps, but it does little work for this claim.

otherClaim.title: Seventy-three per cent of Melbourne apartments built since 2019 provided exactly the legal minimum number of car spaces

claimItself.title: Seventy-three per cent of Melbourne apartments built since 2019 provided exactly the legal minimum number of car spaces
claimItself.oneLiner: If most buildings sit at the floor, the floor is binding.
claimItself.body: Grattan found that since 2019, 73 per cent of Melbourne apartments and 70 per cent of townhouses were built with precisely the minimum parking the rules required. A rule that most projects would exceed anyway would not show this pattern; one that most projects would undercut if allowed does.
